# The Small and Simple Things

Good morning, brothers and sisters. I'm grateful to be asked to speak today, and I'm grateful for each of you. When the bishop called me last week, he gave me a topic and a gentle warning that I should keep to my time. I'll do my best on both counts.

My topic is the small and simple things. In Alma 37:6, Alma teaches his son Helaman, "by small and simple things are great things brought to pass; and small means in many instances doth confound the wise." I've thought about that verse many times this week, and I'd like to share three ways I've seen it come true in my own life.

[pause]

## Small things in the home

The first is in the home. When I was a boy, my family was not what anyone would call a model family. We were loud, we were late to everything, and we argued about whose turn it was to do the dishes. But my mother had one habit she never let go of. Every night, no matter how tired she was, she gathered us in the front room and we read a single chapter of scripture together. Sometimes it was only a few verses before somebody fell asleep on the carpet.

I didn't think much of it at the time. Honestly, I thought it was a little bit boring. But years later, when I was far from home and struggling, I found that those words were still there. They had been planted quietly, one night at a time, and they came back to me when I needed them most.

In Isaiah 28:10, the Lord describes how he teaches us: "precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little." That is exactly how my mother taught us. She never gave a grand lecture. She just kept showing up, here a little and there a little.

Parents, if you're worried that your family scripture study doesn't seem to be working, please don't give up. The results may not show for years. The seeds you plant tonight may not sprout until your children are grown and living far away. But they will sprout.

## Small things in service

The second place I've seen this principle is in service. A few winters ago, our family went through a hard season. I lost my job in November, and by January we were worried about how we would make the mortgage payment. We didn't tell many people. We were embarrassed, and we didn't want anyone to fuss over us.

One cold morning I walked outside to shovel the driveway and found that someone had already done it. The walk was clear, the steps were salted, and there was a loaf of homemade bread wrapped in a towel on the porch. There was no note. To this day I don't know for certain who did it.

That bread did not pay our mortgage. The shoveling did not find me a new job. But I cannot describe how much it lifted us. It told us that someone saw us and that we were not forgotten. It reminded me of what King Benjamin taught in Mosiah 2:17: "when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God."

I've come to believe that most of the Lord's work is done this way. It isn't done in big programs or dramatic rescues. It's done by ordinary people who notice something and quietly do something about it. A text message. A ride to the doctor. A loaf of bread on a cold porch.

The Savior himself taught this. In Matthew 25:40 he says, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." He didn't say inasmuch as ye have done something impressive. He said the least of these. The small, overlooked moments are where he chooses to be found.

[pause]

## Small things in faith

The third place I've seen small and simple things at work is in my own faith. There was a period in my twenties when I wasn't sure what I believed. I had questions I couldn't answer, and the people around me didn't seem to have the answers either. I kept going to church, mostly out of habit, but I felt like I was going through the motions.

During that time I came across the words of Alma in Alma 32:27. He says, "if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you."

A particle of faith. Even if you can no more than desire to believe. When I read that, I realized I didn't have to have everything figured out. I just had to want to believe, and to let that small desire work in me.

So I tried an experiment. I decided that every morning for thirty days I would pray, even if the prayer felt empty, and I would read one page of the Book of Mormon. Just one page. I wrote it on a sticky note and put it on the bathroom mirror.

Nothing dramatic happened on day one, or day ten, or even day thirty. There was no lightning bolt. But somewhere in those weeks, something changed. The prayers stopped feeling empty. The questions didn't all go away, but they stopped feeling like walls. They started feeling like doors.

Alma describes this, too. In Alma 32:28 he says that when the seed is good, "it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves, it must needs be that this is a good seed." That's what it felt like for me. Not a sudden answer, but a slow swelling.

## Why the Lord works this way

You might ask why the Lord works through such small means. Wouldn't it be easier if he just sent an angel to every doubting heart? I've wondered about that.

I think part of the answer is in 1 Kings 19:11–12. Elijah is hiding on the mountain, discouraged and alone. The Lord tells him to stand and watch. A great wind comes and breaks the rocks, but the Lord is not in the wind. Then an earthquake, but the Lord is not in the earthquake. Then a fire, but the Lord is not in the fire. And after the fire, a still small voice.

The Lord could speak in the wind. He could speak in the earthquake. But he chooses the still small voice, because a voice like that can only be heard by someone who is paying attention. Small and simple things require us to be still and to listen. They draw us closer, rather than overwhelming us.

There's another reason, I think. Small things are things we can actually do. Very few of us will ever be asked to do something heroic. But every one of us can read a page, say a prayer, shovel a driveway, or send a kind word. The Lord has made the path to him something that a tired parent, a struggling student, or a lonely widow can walk, one small step at a time.

[pause]

## An invitation

So I'd like to leave you with an invitation. This week, choose one small and simple thing. Just one. It might be reading a chapter with your family, even if somebody falls asleep. It might be noticing a neighbor who is having a hard time and doing something quietly to help. It might be starting your own thirty-day experiment, with a sticky note on the mirror.

Don't worry if it feels too small to matter. That's the whole point. As Alma promised, by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.

I want to bear my testimony that I know this is true. I've seen it in my mother's front room, on a cold porch in January, and in my own heart. I know that our Heavenly Father is aware of each of us, and that he works in our lives through small moments that are easy to miss but impossible to forget. I'm grateful for the Savior, who noticed the least of these, and who invites us to do the same.

I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
